item.title: Will Republicans or Democrats win the Senate? These key midterm races will decide.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Control of both chambers of Congress is up for grabs in November's election. But as important as the House of Representatives is, all signs point to the true drama of the midterms being in the battle for the Senate. There are 35 Senate seats on the ballot this year. Most of those races won't be competitive. The balance of power in the Senate will be decided by the dozen or so states where the outcome truly is uncertain. Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority, which means they can lose three seats and still maintain control of the chamber — thanks to Vice President JD Vance's constitutionally granted power to break ties in an evenly split Senate. Forecasters widely expect Democrats to flip the House, but view the Senate as a "true toss-up." The key Senate battlegrounds include traditional swing states, idiosyncratic areas of the Northeast and historically Republican states where Democrats have rarely been competitive in recent elections. The outcome will have enormous implications for the final two years of President Trump's tenure in the White House. Democrats only need to gain control of one chamber to have the power to block or reshape Trump's legislative agenda. But a Senate majority would empower them to do much more. They would have an effective veto over Trump's nominees for high-ranking Cabinet positions and could block him from appointing any new Supreme Court justices. Control over key Senate committees would also allow Democrats to launch sweeping investigations into Trump and his administration. Here's a rundown of the races that will likely decide which party controls the Senate after the midterms. Alaska Democrat Mary Peltola and Republican Dan Sullivan Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: Amanda Andrade-Rhoades/AP, Greg Nash/Pool via Reuters Party control : GOP The Republican : Dan Sullivan The Democrat : Mary Peltola True to the state's image, there's a wildness to Alaska's Senate race that you won't find elsewhere in the country. On paper, incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan should be well-positioned to win a third term in the Senate. Alaska is a consistently red state that has only elected a Democrat to the Senate once in the past 45 years. Democrats' challenges in the state have been so acute recently that they didn't even have a candidate on the ballot the last time Sullivan was up for reelection. Yahoo But forecasters expect this year's race to be much closer. Sullivan's main opponent is former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola , who was Alaska's lone member of the House from 2022 to 2025. Peltola, the first Alaska Native and first woman to represent the Last Frontier in Congress, is a rare Democrat with a record of success in statewide elections. Sen. Sullivan's path to reelection is also complicated by the presence of a long-shot candidate who shares his name, Dan J. Sullivan, who will also appear on the ballot — potentially creating confusion over which Sullivan voters intend to support. Florida Democrat Angie Nixon and Republican Ashley Moody Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: Joe Raedle/Getty Images, Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images Party control : GOP The Republican : Ashley Moody The Democrat : Angie Nixon It would likely take a major blue wave election for incumbent Republican Sen. Ashley Moody to be at a real risk of being unseated by progressive Democrat Angie Nixon. The GOP has won the last two Senate races in Florida by an average of 14 points. Polls have shown Nixon trailing by a smaller margin than that, but still far enough behind for forecasters to rate the race as favoring Republicans. Georgia Democrat Jon Ossoff and Republican Mike Collins Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: Brynn Anderson/AP, Jason Allen/Getty Images Party control : Democratic The Republican : Mike Collins The Democrat : Jon Ossoff On top of flipping a handful of GOP-held seats, Democrats' chances of gaining control of the Senate rely on keeping the ones they already have. One of the most important is in Georgia. Sen. Jon Ossoff became a rising star within the Democratic Party when he pulled off a stunning upset in the 2020 elections, defeating incumbent Republican David Perdue in an extremely tight runoff. Ossoff is now running for reelection for the first time. His opponent is Rep. Mike Collins, a MAGA-friendly congressman who has created controversy with a series of divisive social media posts during his tenure in the House. More recently, Collins has faced intense scrutiny over his social media posts and the online activity of people close to him , including his son-in-law . Polls have shown Ossoff with a healthy lead over Collins, enough of a gap that forecasters at the non-partisan Center for Politics wrote in July that it would be a "true shock" if he isn't reelected. Iowa Democrat Josh Turek and Republican Ashley Hinson Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: Scott Olson/Getty Images, Charlie Neibergall/Getty Images Party control : GOP The Republican : Ashley Hinson The Democrat : Josh Turek It wasn't that long ago that Iowa was viewed as one of the country's quintessential swing states, but the Hawkeye State has shifted significantly to the right over the past decade — to the point where it's no longer competitive in presidential elections. That said, polls suggest Democrats appear to have a real chance of flipping the Senate seat held by retiring incumbent Joni Ernst. Their nominee is Josh Turek, a state lawmaker and two-time Paralympic gold medalist. A moderate who describes himself as a "prairie populist," Turek has focused heavily on how Trump's tariffs and the war with Iran have affected farmers in his state throughout the campaign. His opponent is GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson, a former local news anchor who cruised to the Republican nomination after earning Trump's endorsement. Polling of the race has fluctuated significantly, with both candidates showing small leads at different times. Kansas Democrat Adam Hamilton and Republican Roger Marshall Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: Emily Curiel/The Kansas City Star/Tribune News Service via Getty Images, Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images Party control : GOP The Republican : Roger Marshall The Democrat : Adam Hamilton It has been almost 100 years since Kansas elected a Democrat to the Senate, but the state may be in play this year as incumbent Republican Roger Marshall looks to keep the GOP's nearly century-long winning streak alive. His opponent is Adam Hamilton, a pastor and the founder of the nation's largest United Methodist church. Forecasters are split on whether Marshall is still the favorite to win, or if the race should be considered a toss-up . Either way, the outcome looks to be on track to be much closer than Republicans are used to in the Sunflower State. Independent voters have favored Hamilton by a large margin in recent surveys. Libertarian Party candidate David Graham is also on the ballot and has drawn a small but potentially significant share of support in some polls. Maine Democrat Troy Jackson and Republican Susan Collins Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: Robert F. Bukaty/AP, Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images Party control : GOP The Republican : Susan Collins The Democrat : Troy Jackson Democrats have been eyeing Sen. Susan Collins's seat for decades, but the Republican has fended off every challenger they've sent her way during her 30 years in the Senate. Her opponent this time around will be Troy Jackson , a former logger and longtime member of the state legislature. Jackson was chosen at a hastily planned convention after the party's original nominee, Graham Platner, dropped out of the race following an allegation of sexual assault, which he denied, among other controversies. Collins has historically managed to outperform other Republicans when she's been on the ballot, even in "blue wave" years like 2020, in part because of her longstanding reputation as a relative moderate within her party. But that image is being tested in this race. Jackson has centered much of his campaign on tying Collins to some of the more high-profile times she's sided with the president on major issues, particularly her votes to confirm Supreme Court justices who later joined the majority in overturning Roe v. Wade . Jackson faces his own challenges. He is playing catch-up after becoming the nominee so late in the process. He will also face scrutiny over his past conservative positions on issues like abortion and same-sex marriage, which are a far cry from the progressive political views he expresses today. Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: Slaven Vlasic/Getty Images, Jeff Kowalsky/AFP via Getty Images Party control : Democratic The Republican : Mike Rogers The Democrat : Abdul El-Sayed One of the nation's few genuine swing states is home to one of the most pivotal midterm matchups. Incumbent Democrat Gary Peters opted not to run for a third term, setting the stage for a nailbiter of a Democratic primary in which progressive physician Abdul El-Sayed narrowly defeated Rep. Haley Stevens, a relative moderate, in a major victory for the party's left wing. There was far less drama on the Republican side, where former Rep. Mike Rogers cruised to the GOP nomination. Rogers was also the Republican nominee in 2024, losing to Democrat Elissa Slotkin by 0.34 percentage points of the vote in one of the tightest Senate races in the country. El-Sayed, who supports policies like a billionaire's tax and Medicare for All, will need the support of centrist Democrats and swing voters in order to build a big enough coalition to win what polls suggest could be another extremely close general election. Minnesota Democrat Peggy Flanagan and Republican Michele Tafoya Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: Abbie Parr/AP, Ellen Schmidt/AP Party control : Democratic The Republican : Michele Tafoya The Democrat : Peggy Flanagan Incumbent Sen. Tina Smith has opted not to run for a second term, which could help create an opening for Republicans to break Democrats' longstanding hold on Minnesota's U.S. Senate delegation. To pursue that goal, the GOP has enlisted a rare political newcomer with widespread name recognition: Former sports broadcaster Michele Tafoya. Her Democratic opponent is Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan. The race so far has been defined by the remarkably different approaches of the two candidates. Tafoya has worked to push her party toward the political center, portraying herself as a moderate Republican and mostly focusing on issues like affordability and public safety while steering clear of some of the more divisive parts of Trump's agenda. Flanagan, on the other hand, is a progressive who represents a significant step to the left on policy for Democrats relative to Smith. Polls have suggested that the race could be extremely close . Nebraska Independent Dan Osborn and Republican Pete Ricketts Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images, Alex Brandon/AP Party control : GOP The Republican : Pete Ricketts The independent : Dan Osborn In a state as red as Nebraska, rather than fielding their own candidate to challenge incumbent Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts, Democrats have thrown their support behind independent candidate Dan Osborn. This is the second time that Osborn, a Navy veteran and former labor union leader, has run for the Senate in a race without a Democratic candidate. Two years ago, he finished about 6 points behind GOP Sen. Deb Fisher in the state's closest Senate race in more than two decades. Osborn has been deeply critical of both parties and says he opposes parts of the Democratic Party's platform. But if he's elected, the GOP would lose a Senate seat it currently holds and one vote that it can comfortably count on in support of Trump's legislative agenda. New Hampshire Democrat Chris Pappas and Republican John E. Sununu Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images, Sophie Park/Getty Images Party control : Democratic The Republican : John Sununu The Democrat : Chris Pappas The Granite State is rarely discussed as a swing state because it consistently votes for Democrats in presidential elections. But Senate races are a different story. Several Republicans have been elected to represent New Hampshire in the Senate in recent decades. One of them is John Sununu, who is running to regain the seat he lost in 2008 when he was defeated by Democrat Jeanne Shaheen, the retiring incumbent. Sununu is part of a political dynasty in the state. His father, also named John, and his brother Chris both served as governor. The Democratic nominee is Rep. Chris Pappas, a moderate who comfortably outpaced a democratic socialist rival in his party's primary. Pappas is the first gay man to represent New Hampshire in Congress and would become the first openly gay male senator in U.S. history if he is elected. North Carolina Democrat Roy Cooper and Republican Michael Whatley Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: Allen G. Breed/AP, Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images Party control : GOP The Republican : Michael Whatley The Democrat : Roy Cooper If polls are accurate, Republicans have a lot of ground to make up if they want to hold on to this seat from the Tarheel State. Incumbent Sen. Thom Tillis, a rare member of the GOP caucus to defy the president in some circumstances, has opted not to seek reelection. The Republican nominee to replace him is Michael Whatley, a former chair of the Republican National Committee. Whatley has a strong history in North Carolina, having run the state Republican Party for nearly five years, but he lacks the statewide name recognition of his Democratic opponent, former Gov. Roy Cooper. Both of Cooper's gubernatorial wins were reasonably close, but polls have shown him with a significant lead over Whatley. Forecasters have also shifted the race toward Democrats. Ohio Democrat Sherrod Brown and Republican Jon Husted Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: Jeff Dean/AP, Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Party control : GOP The Republican : Jon Husted The Democrat : Sherrod Brown The Buckeye State has trended to the right over the past decade or so, but a unique set of circumstances has contributed to making this race a genuine toss-up in the eyes of some forecasters. Aside from the Democratic and Republican nominees, Libertarian William Redpath and Greg Levy of the Party for Socialism and Liberation are also on the ballot. These two lesser-known candidates are getting as much as 6% of voters' support in polls, collectively, which is potentially enough to influence the outcome in a very tight race. Husted is the rare incumbent with less experience than his challenger. He has only been in the Senate since 2025, when he was appointed to fill the vacancy created when JD Vance became vice president. Brown, on the other hand, served three full terms in the Senate before losing his seat to Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024. Brown also has a massive cash advantage, which has allowed his campaign to spend more than four times as much as Husted's so far, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Despite all of that, Brown is still swimming upstream in a state that has become solidly red over the past few election cycles. South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews and Republican Darline Graham Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: Sean Rayford/Getty Images Party control : GOP The Republican : Darline Graham The Democrat : Annie Andrews The word "competitive" is rarely used to describe statewide races in a place as red as South Carolina, but the death of longtime incumbent Sen. Lindsey Graham in July has set up what could be the Palmetto State's first tight Senate race in a generation. Graham's sister, Darline Graham, was appointed to finish the rest of his term and is now running for a full six-year term. Her opponent is Democrat Annie Andrews, a pediatrician who has staked out several policy positions that reflect the state's conservatism, including support for the Second Amendment, tax cuts and strong immigration enforcement. Republicans have comfortably won every Senate election in South Carolina since the early 2000s, but Trump's declining approval rating in the state and apparent concerns about Graham's lack of experience have likely contributed to making this a much closer race. Recent polls have shown Andrews trailing by as little as a single point, though forecasters still list the state as a likely Republican victory. Texas Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: Brenda Bazán/AP, Tony Gutierrez/AP Party control : GOP The Republican : Ken Paxton The Democrat : James Talarico Republicans haven't lost a statewide election in the Lone Star State in more than three decades, but forecasters say Democratic state lawmaker James Talarico has a chance of ending that streak in November. His Republican opponent is Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who defeated longtime incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in a tightly contested and often contentious Republican primary. Paxton has faced serious legal issues during his tenure as Texas's top law enforcement official, including accusations of corruption that led the state House to impeach him in 2023. The state Senate later acquitted him on all articles it considered. Polls have consistently shown a tight contest , with a good number finding Talarico leading by a small margin. item.title: House speaker's wife ministers to Hill staffers, but nonprofit funding is a mystery
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
After House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-Louisiana) ascended to one of the most powerful offices in Washington three years ago, his wife, a faith-based counselor, turned her focus to the nation’s capital. Kelly Johnson reoriented a religious nonprofit she was running back home in the Shreveport area into a ministry focused on female congressional staffers. Its new purpose, according to an IRS filing, was to help “the hundreds of unreached young women” working around Capitol Hill “find purpose, belonging, and Christian community.” Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Through the organization, a part-time endeavor run solely by Johnson, she provides counseling, delivers speeches and conducts “spiritual heritage tours” of the U.S. Capitol that highlight the nation’s Christian history. In 2024, financial disclosures show Johnson was paid $50,000 for 10 hours of work per week. The nonprofit, Onward Christian Education Services, has become part of the rising presence in official Washington of evangelical Christianity as its devotees, a key bloc of support for President Donald Trump, seek to inject a biblical worldview into American politics and government. The centerpiece of Johnson’s organization is the faith-based counseling that she said she provides free to staff and the spouses of House members. “I’m a missionary here,” Johnson said in an interview. “It’s kind of a calling in this life for me,” she added. “This is what I love to do. This is my heart.” The full extent of Kelly Johnson’s work in Washington is unclear, however. Some mysteries remain about her organization, including who is funding it. Onward Christian Education Services brought in an average of more than $60,000 in contributions annually during its early years. Donors are disclosed to the IRS but redacted in publicly available filings. Johnson said her nonprofit has “several large benefactors,” whom she described as “primarily just individuals who have an interest in this and have a heart in this.” She would not name them or disclose whether they are also supporters of her husband’s political campaigns, and she declined to voluntarily provide unredacted filings to The Washington Post. The publicly available records contain inconsistencies and omissions. Johnson, who IRS filings indicate also does the bookkeeping, has occasionally revised annual revenue figures for previous years without explanation. On a 2023 annual form, she neglected to report her own salary, which accounts for almost 90 percent of spending since the organization formed. The Post spoke to four people who work on nonprofit law and government ethics. They stressed there’s nothing wrong with the purpose of Onward Christian Education Services but raised concerns about how Kelly Johnson’s close connection to the speaker’s office could benefit the nonprofit. “It should make everyone uncomfortable that the speaker’s wife would be raising money for a mission to serve congressional staff,” said Meredith McGehee, a former lobbyist for several nonpartisan groups that advocate for campaign finance transparency and anti-corruption measures in government. “It really dances on that blurred line of separation of church and state and using public resources for private interests.” In a statement, Mike Johnson praised his wife’s ministry work and Christian counseling services as life-changing for many. “She has a true gift with people and has inspired many other women to live out their faith, overcome their obstacles, and find peace and success, even in an environment as challenging as Capitol Hill,” he said. Kelly Johnson has intentionally tried to keep her nonprofit’s second chapter out of the spotlight after what she considered an unfairly hostile reception to the couple’s religious views when Mike Johnson became speaker in October 2023. Onward Christian Education Services previously operated for five years in Louisiana. The Post discovered the change in mission when a reporter requested recent IRS filings for the group, which had not filed legally required disclosures for tax-exempt organizations for two years. Kelly Johnson submitted the organization’s 2024 filing after the inquiry, revealing its new purpose, though she did not explain the delay. A spokesperson said Johnson requested an extension for her 2025 IRS filing and has not yet completed it. The form is typically due in May and nonprofits can ask for a six-month extension. After an initial interview, Johnson declined to speak to a reporter again. The Post has pieced together this portrait of Onward Christian Education Services through that conversation, an analysis of available public documents and written questions submitted to Mike Johnson’s office. The Johnsons were ordained as Southern Baptist missionaries more than two decades ago, and in 2017, their church in Benton, Louisiana, formally ordained Kelly Johnson as a minister. The same year, she was licensed as a pastoral counselor through the National Christian Counselors Association, opening a practice at the church. Though she has never held elected office herself, Johnson has also long been politically active. Two decades ago, when Mike Johnson was still a practicing attorney, the couple were vocal advocates for covenant marriage, a legal union with more limited standing for divorce, and participated in an interview with Diane Sawyer about their experience. Kelly Johnson has previously worked for Louisiana Right to Life, an antiabortion advocacy group. She was intimately involved in her husband’s political rise. In 2022, the couple started a podcast together covering “hot topics and current events from a Christian perspective,” which they hosted until Mike Johnson became speaker. Onward Christian Education Services was created as a tax-exempt organization in April 2019 to counter what the Johnsons described at the time as cultural attacks against people of faith and the traditional family. Kelly Johnson recently told The Post she came to see that education was important. “People have forgotten our history and our Christian heritage,” she said. “For a long time, I felt that burden.” The purpose of the nonprofit, according to early tax filings, was to “empower Christians to follow the Biblical commands to understand and meet the challenges of our day,” primarily through live seminars at churches across Louisiana and eventually other states. Kelly Johnson served as the CEO and the only employee. “Mike and Kelly Johnson ‘rang the bell’ to awaken our people to become Christian patriots,” Gevan Spinney, a local pastor who serves as president of Onward Christian Education Services’ board, told the Baptist Message, a faith-based publication, in an article that May touting the seminar. Onward Christian Education Services initially did not submit any filings to the IRS. In 2022, when Kelly Johnson submitted forms for the first three years of operation, she blamed “a communication gap and misunderstanding of the filing requirements” for a nonprofit so closely affiliated with a religious denomination. The organization paid $6,475 in penalties to the Treasury Department. From 2019 to 2023, Johnson reported working 10 hours a week for Onward Christian Education Services, earning between $35,383 and $64,485 annually. During the covid-19 pandemic, the organization developed prerecorded presentations of its seminars. The Johnsons’ podcast followed. Once her husband became speaker, Kelly Johnson said, the couple had to spend more time in Washington and were no longer able to conduct regular church visits. So in 2024, she transitioned the focus of her nonprofit to the capital, folding in her counseling business and offering free sessions. Johnson said she has 10 or 11 clients, whom she counsels through a lens of spirituality and the Bible about the issues that women face, including anxiety and depression, adjusting to a new city and problems with their families. The organization maintains a low profile because, Johnson said, she fears for her safety. Her clients come through word of mouth, rather than advertising, Johnson said, and unlike in Louisiana, where she had an office at her church, they meet for counseling sessions at home or over FaceTime. “People want things to be private,” she said. “If I had an office, there would likely be protesters outside of it. I would like to have an office. Boy, would I like to.” Taylor Haulsee, a spokesman for Mike Johnson, said in a statement that “no House Republican Caucus or member office has ever been used for” outreach to staffers and that most of the nonprofit’s activities take place away from the Capitol complex. Other programming since Onward Christian Education Services shifted to Washington has included Kelly Johnson speaking at a Christian women’s conference in Kentucky in 2024, leading the spiritual heritage tours of the Capitol and organizing a Bible study, which Johnson said was hard to maintain because “people are just so overcommitted.” Johnson turned down a request from The Post for one of her Capitol tours. Haulsee said the tours are within House guidelines and they are “scheduled for small groups of people upon request, which is the same access available to any and all citizens to the People’s House.” He would not share who those people are or what they visit on the tours. As she expanded her ministry into Washington, Johnson teamed up with “like-minded organizations operating in the nation’s capital such as Concerned Women for America, Inc.,” according to the 2024 IRS filing. Concerned Women for America is an advocacy group “dedicated to impacting the culture for Christ through education and public policy,” according to its website. A spokesperson declined to answer questions about the organization’s work with Johnson. Government ethics advocates said the lack of transparency surrounding Onward Christian Education Services means the public cannot be certain whether donors are using the organization to gain access to the Johnsons or whether Kelly Johnson receives advantages, such as access to the Capitol for her tours, that other nonprofits could not get. “Is it serving a political purpose or is it serving an actual charity?” said Philip Hackney, a professor at the University of Pittsburgh School of Law who specializes in nonprofit law. Without proper safeguards, young staffers could also feel pressured to participate in Johnson’s counseling and Bible study, said Davina Hurt, director of the government ethics program at Santa Clara University’s Markkula Center for Applied Ethics. She said it would be helpful to know who extends the invitations, whether the speaker’s name gets invoked and whether attendance is ever shared with the boss of a Hill staffer. “The institutional concern one should have is the power that’s present in those situations,” Hurt said. “If you want to advance through the ranks, you will feel pressure to some degree.” Haulsee said no staffers have ever been pressured to participate in Johnson’s programming. McGehee, the former ethics lobbyist, said she is sympathetic to the challenges a prominent politician’s spouse faces figuring out an appropriate role in Washington. But Onward Christian Education Services should at least articulate a firmer wall between Johnson and the money, she said, to avoid even the appearance of conflicts of interest. McGehee questioned why Johnson needed to be paid at all to minister to congressional staffers. “This is not about the value of the work,” McGehee said. “But it’s fraught.” In 2024, an IRS filing shows that Johnson took a salary of $50,000 even though the organization brought in no revenue that year, depleting its reserves to $5,797. Johnson said she was too busy with her husband’s new position to fundraise. The 2024 filing is the most recent financial statement available. Johnson deferred to her four-member board on questions about her salary. Three of its members, who have all been in their positions since Onward Christian Education Services began, did not respond to attempts by The Post to speak with them. Board Secretary Julianna Parks, an attorney and local government official in Bossier Parish, Louisiana, said they set Johnson’s salary annually by looking at what other nonprofit directors in the area make. The Johnsons “insisted that it not be excessive in any way,” she said. “So we always erred on the lower side.” Parks said she first met Mike Johnson professionally through the local law community and became friendly with the Johnsons when their children attended the same private Christian school. She declined to discuss any other specifics of the organization or how the board operates, including whether it had advised Kelly Johnson as she refocused her work to Washington. “I don’t really feel comfortable answering specifically to this organization,” Parks said. She said that she thought a story about Onward Christian Education Services was a bad idea because she did not want to put a spotlight on the Johnson family during a dangerous time in the country. item.title: Jon Ossoff shuts down 2028 presidential speculation in heated Georgia Senate debate
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., speaking in September. (Elijah Nouvelage / Getty) Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., said Tuesday night during a debate that he will not run for president in 2028. Ossoff made the statement in response to a question as he faced off with his Republican challenger, Rep. Mike Collins. Ossoff is seeking a second six-year term in Georgia and said he would serve the full term. “I have zero interest in running for president,” Ossoff said when he was asked directly by one of the moderators. “I’m not running for president. I’m running for re-election to the Senate.” Ossoff has been regularly discussed as a potential Democratic contender in 2028. If he were to win the presidency, he would have to give up his Senate seat, which he stressed Tuesday night that he would not do. After the brief remark, Ossoff quickly transitioned to pressing Collins about why he has supported President Donald Trump’s tariffs, a main focus of both his campaign and a debate the two held last week . Tuesday was the second debate in the nationally watched Georgia Senate race, this one organized by the Atlanta Press Club. Collins quipped that Ossoff was actually trying to run for president and will be “your DSA candidate,” a reference to the Democratic Socialists of America. The exchange came at the beginning of the hourlong debate, which covered ground including data centers; the economy under Trump, whose approval rating is at record lows; the war in Iran; and the issue of Collins’ son-in-law’s promoting white nationalist posts on social media. Ossoff asked Collins directly whether he considered himself a “white nationalist.” “I condemn any sort of hate speech,” Collins said. “Antisemitism, hate of any kind. It’s abhorrent.” The exchange continued when Collins again asked Ossoff to denounce Reid Hoffman, a major donor to Democratic causes — including Ossoff-aligned political committees — whose name appeared in the Epstein files . Collins brought up Hoffman several times last week and did so again during the second debate. Ossoff did not directly respond, and he again pointed to the fact that those close to Collins amplified white nationalists’ posts. “How weak a person do you have to be to be unable to stop someone under your own roof from disseminating neo-Nazi propaganda while you run for Senate?” Ossoff said. “The paper reported it’s still going on today.” Given a chance to respond, Collins did not address it directly. But he said rhetoric like Ossoff’s had motivated a New York man who is accused of making death threats against him. “I’m a little tired of this, Jon,” Collins said. “This crazy person is in jail right now because of your rhetoric.” Neither candidate directly answered the other’s charges. Collins also, once again, did not answer questions about whether or not Joe Biden won the 2020 presidential election. He was asked about audio of a call Trump made after the 2020 election asking Georgia Republican Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger to “ find 11,780 votes ” to help overturn the 2020 election. “You know, Joe Biden went into office, and boy, Georgians paid for it,” Collins said. item.title: Some peptide users report lasting symptoms as RFK Jr. pushes for wider access
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
After the third day of squirting an experimental drug up his nose, Dylan Meetze felt horrible. "It was like I was underwater, like it took the most to do anything," he said. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Meetze stopped taking the drug, but he endured fatigue and anxiety for months afterward, and his eyes and muscles twitched, he said. He had taken BPC-157, a peptide drug popularized by podcasts about wellness, longevity and what's called "body optimization." Peptide is a general term for substances that are smaller than proteins but composed of the same building blocks. Dozens of peptide drugs, including insulin and GLP-1 weight loss medicines, have garnered approval by the Food and Drug Administration. But BPC-157 and many others have not because they haven't undergone clinical trials. This fact hasn't stopped online influencers from promoting them as remedies for muscle injuries, gut issues, covid and more. Use of BPC-157 is growing in the United States, particularly among White males, according to a new analysis of millions of de-identified electronic health records. Since 2020, the analysis, which hasn't yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal, found that more than 1,000 people told doctors they had used the drug. Meetze said he decided to take BPC-157 after listening to Andrew Huberman, a Stanford neuroscientist with more than 16 million followers on YouTube, Instagram and TikTok, who talks up peptides frequently on his podcasts. Studies in mice suggest that BPC-157 helps muscles heal and has "very high safety profiles," Huberman has said, "at least, with respect to the lethal dosing." His guest on one episode, Craig Koniver, a doctor who sells peptides through his wellness clinic, called BPC-157 "super safe" and recommended it for "anyone who's working out on a regular basis." Koniver did not respond to requests for comment. Huberman didn't respond to multiple queries from KFF Health News, but an automatic reply linked to a disclaimer on his Huberman Lab website that says the podcast doesn't constitute medical advice: "Any reliance on information provided through the podcast is solely at the user's own risk." Hoping BPC-157 might help him advance as a weightlifter, Meetze said he bought the drug last year from an online vendor, Researchem. A chemical supply company with that name sells experimental peptides through its website, warning that the substances are "solely for laboratory research" and are "not intended for human consumption." (It lists an address in Hillsboro, Oregon, that corresponds to a shared office space. A receptionist at the space said Researchem wasn't registered there, and multiple queries from KFF Health News to the email address listed on the website went unanswered.) Companies are required to warn that experimental peptides, which haven't been approved by the FDA, are for research use only. But many companies may soon be permitted to drop the warning because of a push by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to lower barriers to their use. He and other leaders of the Make America Healthy Again movement have promoted peptides as a way to improve the country's health. On X, before he took the helm at the Department of Health and Human Services, Kennedy vowed to end the "aggressive suppression" of "peptides, stem cells, raw milk" and "anything else that advances human health and can't be patented by Pharma." (In fact, peptides are heavily patented.) He has repeated the pledge since taking office. On Joe Rogan's podcast early this year, Kennedy said he was a "big fan" of peptides and wanted to make many of them "more accessible." On a podcast with the co-chair of the MAHA Action committee, Gary Brecka, Kennedy said the FDA's role should be to assess science, "but not tell people and not tell physicians what they can and cannot prescribe." "If you want to take an experimental drug … you ought to be able to do that," he added. This summer, Kennedy's health department appointed doctors with financial stakes in the peptide industry to a panel that advises the FDA. At an FDA meeting in July, the new appointees voted to ease restrictions on six experimental peptides, including the trendy compounds BPC-157, TB-500 and MOTS-c. They advised adding these peptides to a list, called 503A, that would allow specialized pharmacies to make the drugs for human use, even though the FDA hasn't approved them. In an email, HHS spokesperson Emily Hilliard wrote that every committee member satisfies the FDA's ethics requirements. "FDA - not podcasts or politics - determines which substances qualify for inclusion on the 503A Bulks List," she wrote. The FDA has yet to issue a final decision. The vote went against FDA scientists who presented research on the six peptides, concluding there wasn't enough evidence to show that they improved any condition. Furthermore, the scientists highlighted a potential for liver damage, allergic reactions or other serious consequences. "People are saying this is about medical freedom - putting decisions back in the hands of patients," said Reshma Ramachandran, a regulatory science researcher at Yale School of Medicine. "But what we see in practice is that incentives aren't actually centered around patients. They're centered around selling products." Scientists also warned that drugmakers would be reluctant to invest millions of dollars into clinical trials on peptides if they could be sold without FDA approval. "The chances of clinical trials getting done now are diminished," said Eric Topol, executive vice president of Scripps Research, a biomedical science institute in San Diego. "We will have more people who are prey to predators that will sell, sell, sell." A lack of data leaves consumers in the dark. Meetze sought help on Reddit, where people post about pain, headaches, vision problems and a lack of motivation after taking experimental peptides. Peptide enthusiasts often comment on these posts with skepticism, attributing a person's problems to contaminated products, preexisting conditions or misuse of the drugs. The online vitriol can be intense, so Meetze welcomed an invitation to join a private group on the social platform Discord, in which people with BPC-157 side effects tried to figure out what happened to them and how to fix it. "There are millions of success stories with these peptides," Meetze said, "but no one wants to believe that this wrecks some of our lives." Reports of side effects One member of the private side-effects group, a 46-year-old software engineer named Dominik E., said he got an excruciating migraine within days of taking BPC-157 with TB-4, another unapproved peptide - a combination called the "Wolverine stack" because of its purported ability to heal wounds rapidly like its namesake Marvel superhero. "My left eye started throbbing really badly, and the left side of my face became numb," he told KFF Health News, which agreed to only partially identify him and others interviewed for this article who were concerned about divulging sensitive health information. After two months of migraines, Dominik said, the pain eased, but his face felt inflamed. "It is a total nightmare," he said. "I'm afraid how people will judge me," said Lois S., a woman who works at a Michigan elementary school. She hoped BPC-157 and another unapproved peptide, retatrutide, would help with weight loss, but she stopped taking the treatment when she felt pain. "I sought out this substance from a lab that clearly labeled it not for human use, purchased a syringe, and injected this in my kitchen," she said. "That belies all logic about what a normal person would do." Peptide proponents argue that shoddy manufacturing - not the peptides - causes harm. Therefore, they say, the FDA must protect the public by allowing doctors to prescribe peptides made for human use by pharmacies that specialize in compounding medicines. Typically, compounding pharmacies manufacture alternatives to FDA-approved drugs: for example, so that a patient can get a liquid version of a drug that the original manufacturer makes only as pills. Adding unapproved peptides to the FDA's list of compoundable drugs would mark a departure from the list's purpose, said Peter Lurie, a former FDA official who now directs the advocacy group Center for Science in the Public Interest. He said that federal and state oversight for compounding pharmacies is often lax, and the pharmacies have been cited for contamination. Furthermore, he added, the move would mislead consumers into thinking they're buying drugs backed by clinical trials. People promoting peptides often point to promising laboratory research as evidence. Rats with spinal injuries regained tail mobility after BPC-157 injections, for example, and old mice given the experimental peptide MOTS-c could run longer. On average, however, fewer than 10 percent of substances that show promise in animal studies prove effective in clinical trials. "A lot of this pseudoscience stuff sounds deeply impressive - inflammation this and telomere that - but at the end of the day, none of it really matters," Lurie said. "You've got to show clinical benefit in humans: Does it work?" Peptide promoters lean on anecdotes, often without verifiable numbers. In a podcast recorded at the White House, the MAHA influencer Brecka said: "Twenty million people have been prescribed these things without adverse events." His guest on the episode, Brigham Buhler - the co-author of "The Peptide Revolution" and owner of a compounding pharmacy that sells peptides and a clinic, Ways2Well, that prescribes them - told Brecka that none of its 75,000-plus patients had reported adverse events from peptides. Buhler cited even higher numbers in the movie "MAHA Uncensored," a documentary featuring Kennedy and other leaders of the MAHA movement, and that bears the MAHA trademark. In the segment on peptides, Buhler said, "Having treated literally hundreds of thousands of people through our compounding pharmacy, we've never had a major adverse event." Topol asks why those boasting success haven't conducted clinical studies. "If influencers and companies really believe these peptides are helping people," Topol said, "then they should put their profits back into rigorous research." Chris Woodward, a spokesperson for Brecka and his company, the Ultimate Human, said in an email that the health and wellness issues discussed on Brecka's podcast do not constitute medical advice. "Mr. Brecka consistently advises his audience to consult a licensed physician," Woodward wrote. Buhler did not respond to requests for comment. Not all anecdotes are rosy. At an antiaging conference in July 2025 Las Vegas, two women were rushed to the hospital and intubated after being injected with experimental peptides and vitamins at a booth in the exhibit hall, according to citations that Nevada's state pharmacy board issued against the doctor running the booth and his colleagues for prescribing and administering drugs without a state medical license. An FDA database for adverse events contains concerning reports. Although the database can't prove that a drug, vaccine or medical device caused harm - the reports are brief, unverified and voluntary - it signals issues worth exploring. A 36-year-old woman was hospitalized in December after taking BPC-157 for weight control and a skin disorder, for example, and a 48-year-old man was hospitalized with a "life-threatening" condition after taking the peptide. FDA scientists presented some of these reports at the July meeting and flagged worrisome outcomes in animal experiments, such as a 2020 study revealing signs of liver toxicity in rats and dogs injected with BPC-157. Brian Lee, a liver disease specialist at the University of Southern California, was among the panel's minority who voted against easing restrictions. Without clinical studies, he said, afflictions that take time to develop, like liver damage and cancer, might not be spotted for years: "I think this endorsement can be potentially harmful, and I cannot in good conscience vote yes." The panel's newcomers disagreed. "I do not believe the FDA made a good case on issues with safety with BPC," said Kris Wusterhausen, founder of an antiaging company in Texas, the Resurge Clinic, which sells a BPC-157 product for $149. "Once you've seen the effects of BPC," he said, "you can't unsee it." Awaiting trial Deepak Srivastava, president of the Gladstone Institutes in San Francisco, designed a clinical trial two decades ago to see if a peptide he studies, TB-4, could repair tissue after a heart attack. Before enrollment, people volunteering for the study would be screened for early signs of cancer because TB-4 triggers vessel growth and cell migration, which might exacerbate malignant growths. He worries about the FDA panel's vote to ease restrictions on a derivative of TB-4, before such trials have been completed, saying, "You need to have a healthy respect for the fact that drugs can be harmful." Pinchas Cohen, a peptide researcher at the University of Southern California, was less cautious, saying the FDA buzz might drive investors to fund trials. He's seeking support to bring a peptide his lab identified, MOTS-c, to market. It's "un-ideal" for people to take unproven drugs, Cohen said, but that's what's happening: "The world is changing, and people like me need to accept that this is the new reality and find ways to make it as safe as possible." In the meantime, people like Meetze resort to podcasts and online forums for advice. His symptoms faded after a year, but he still had spells of feeling "zero emotions." Peptide users describe this condition as anhedonia. It's come up on Huberman's podcasts. Huberman occasionally mentions other potential peptide risks, like cancer, sprinkling them into advice on how to take them. Take a 2024 episode with 1.2 million views: "I do not think that BPC-157 is not without its quote-unquote 'side effects,'" Huberman says. He adds, "If you're going to go down this path of taking BPC-157, I would encourage you to take the minimal effective dose, to not simply do it every day, and certainly to not do it continuously, and of course to monitor your other health metrics for anything that could potentially resemble cancer or tumor growth, because obviously stimulating angiogenesis for wound repair sounds like a great thing - recovering and being able to do your workouts or play your sport, or move about more comfortably, of course - a wonderfully attractive thing to do." "Isn't that what we all want? But obviously not with the trade-off of growing a tumor," he said, before interrupting the discussion to advertise a supplement company sponsoring the show. item.title: Many GOP lawmakers are losing faith in the party's lame-duck ambitions
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Republicans have had to defer many of their legislative dreams, hoping the post-election release of political pressure could set up a productive “lame duck” session before a new Congress is seated. Fat chance, many GOP lawmakers now say. Beyond the uncertainties surrounding the midterms and a potential transition of power on Capitol Hill, members will return to Washington facing a considerable list of must-pass bipartisan bills but also potentially messy internal leadership fights, a foul national mood and a mere 24 legislative days to get anything done. One thing on Republicans’ minds is whether some of their members even come back to vote . “The question becomes: Who shows up for work after the elections?” Rep. Austin Scott (R-Ga.) said in an interview. “Attendance is an issue right now.” There are some items, Scott added, that “ultimately … have to get done.” Those include an extension of government funding past Dec. 11 and the annual Pentagon policy bill. Major pieces of legislation to reauthorize farm, transportation and surveillance programs are also on deck . All are loaded with potential partisan flash points, however, and won’t be legislative chip shots. Then there are pending bipartisan bills overhauling energy permitting and the college sports industry that many members are itching to get done this year. But many lawmakers fear those could easily get left behind — especially if Democrats can win control of either chamber and seek greater influence on the final products. “What do you think?” an exasperated Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said about the prospect for bipartisan accomplishments in the lame duck. “I mean, why? If you think about it, if Democrats win the House, why would they?” Rep. Dan Newhouse (R-Wash.), who like Tillis is leaving Congress at the end of the year, echoed the belief that Democrats would “want to put their fingerprints more on things before they pass” in a majority-flips scenario. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer suggested as much in a recent interview : “The lame duck will be quite different if we win the Senate,” he said. “Same thing if they win the House, and same thing if we win both or neither.” Then there are partisan GOP priorities that some Republicans are hoping to ram through in the final weeks of the year — especially if the party’s governing trifecta is about to end — such as enacting hundreds of millions of dollars in new defense funding as well as new voting restrictions. While GOP leaders are leaving the door open to attempting to pass another bill through the party-line reconciliation process, there are no signs they are closer to having the necessary votes than they were this summer. While some Republicans believe that losing a chamber would jump-start that process, others privately believe the exact opposite would happen, according to three GOP aides granted anonymity to speak candidly. There will be little incentive for lawmakers who just lost their seats — “free-range chickens,” some call them — to grind out a final legislative win, if they come back at all. Senate Majority Leader John Thune last month admitted he is facing mathematical realities that make passing another reconciliation bill “difficult” even in a lame-duck session. That likely spells doom for another GOP wish being bandied about for the post-midterms session: clearing a debt-limit increase through the end of President Donald Trump’s term. Thune has acknowledged that as a possibility multiple times since July, but several GOP senators are skeptical. “I don't like that idea,” said retiring Sen. Cynthia Lummis (R-Wyo.), who added she had to “hold my nose” in voting for the last debt-ceiling lift. But other GOP leaders are professing more optimism about the post-midterm environment to overcome some long-standing roadblocks. House Majority Leader Steve Scalise in an interview called it “an opportunity for everybody to focus on getting policy done because the election will be over.” “I hope we get back to that, because it needs to happen,” he said. But each piece of legislation still in limbo is riddled with thorny policy disputes. Senate Democrats blocked the defense bill amid a standoff over the Iran war and have objected to giving Trump back some surveillance powers. The farm bill, meanwhile, is mired in a fight over food assistance . Thune has teed up an initial vote on the bipartisan permitting deal , but Democrats continue to doubt whether Trump will live up to GOP negotiators’ clean energy commitments — and they could push for more concessions if they prevail in the midterms. Even the must-do government funding bill is a potential minefield, with lawmakers widely expecting a punt until deeper into the holidays or even next year. Democrats are fuming over the Trump administration’s recent decision to block roughly $1 billion in congressionally approved funding, which could complicate the dealmaking ahead of the deadline. That could make passage of the 12 annual spending bills, or a combined full-year “omnibus” package, impossible. “I just don't think we'll get them done by the 11th,” Rep. Mike Simpson of Idaho, a senior GOP appropriator, said about the full-year bills. He predicted another short-term punt. Beyond the policy disputes, there’s a host of other distractions leaders of both parties will be dealing with once they return to session Nov. 9. Speaker Mike Johnson will immediately have to deal with a House vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth forced by outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.). With the Iran war weighing heavily on voters’ views of the GOP, some Republicans with an eye on the next election could decide to break ranks. And though the elections will be over outside the Capitol, internal politicking could continue for weeks in both chambers. A Democratic flip of the House could spark a potentially chaotic cascade of GOP leadership elections, especially with Johnson giving mixed signals about his intentions in that scenario. He broached the possibility he might not remain atop his conference in a Fox News interview last week, then said in a CBS News interview published Monday that he expected "my colleagues would ask me to continue leading this conference" even after a loss. Thune says he is running again for GOP leader regardless of the election outcome, and no other senator has signaled they will challenge him. That hasn’t stopped some conservatives, in and out of the chamber, from questioning whether Trump will blame him if the majority is lost. Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) said the lame duck to-do list could ultimately come down to vibes. “I know what they would like us to do and all that,” Kennedy said. “But you have no idea what the mood is going to be.” This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/13/gop-lame-duck-reality-check-01114594

item.title: DOJ subpoenas Rep. Ilhan Omar's relatives in immigration probe
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn. (AP) The Justice Department, in an apparent escalation of a long-running investigation involving the immigration history of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., has issued subpoenas to members of her family, The New York Times reported Tuesday, as the congresswoman accuses the Trump administration of political retribution for her outspoken criticism of the president. The subpoenas mark a new development in a probe that has drawn scrutiny after federal agents searched Omar's Washington-area home Monday, an action she condemned as an attempt to intimidate political opponents and weaponize federal law enforcement. "For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns," Omar wrote on social media Monday. "This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced." Federal authorities have not publicly laid out the full scope of the investigation or disclosed what evidence investigators are seeking through the subpoenas. The search Monday was conducted by agents with Homeland Security Investigations under a court-authorized warrant, the Justice Department confirmed, but officials offered few details about the criminal investigation. The inquiry follows months of public comments by Trump administration officials about allegations involving Omar's immigration history. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said last month that an ongoing investigation was examining, in part, whether Omar had lied on immigration forms, adding that "something's going to happen," according to The Associated Press. Omar, who was born in Somalia and became a naturalized U.S. citizen, has repeatedly rejected allegations concerning her immigration history. President Donald Trump has frequently criticized Omar, particularly over her immigration views and opposition to his policies. Trump said Monday he had "nothing to do" with the search, while also calling Omar "totally crooked, personally," according to the AP. The timing of the search has intensified questions about whether the investigation is politically motivated, coming just weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., and other top Democrats condemned the search, accusing the administration of targeting Omar and raising concerns about the use of federal law enforcement against a political opponent. Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, described the action as political harassment and argued that the timing conflicted with longstanding Justice Department practices concerning politically sensitive investigations before elections. Justice Department guidance has traditionally cautioned against overt investigative steps intended to influence an election, although the existence of a search warrant does not itself establish that an investigation is politically motivated. Vice President JD Vance has previously accused Omar of immigration fraud, according to news reports, while the administration has maintained that federal authorities are pursuing an ongoing criminal investigation. Grand jury subpoenas are used to obtain testimony or documents during investigations and do not, by themselves, establish wrongdoing by the people who receive them. The Justice Department has not publicly announced any criminal charges against Omar in connection with the investigation. © 2026 Newsmax. item.title: Zelensky says Ukraine received no early warning from partners about missiles headed to Kyiv
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Ukraine received no early warning from its partners about five Russian ballistic missiles that hit civilian infrastructure in the capital of Kyiv, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Tuesday, as tensions rise between the Ukrainian leader and U.S. President Donald Trump. Zelenskyy did not specify which partners he was talking about. He characterized the barrage as “particularly vile” and emphasized that receiving intelligence from partners about such attacks “helps save lives" and is "one of the most critical issues.” "This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed — when there is an early warning about ballistic missiles,” he wrote in a post on X. Trump said the U.S. has not stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine. “We are helping them, and we are sharing intel,” Trump told reporters at the White House. “We want the war to end, so we’re working with them and with Russia on getting the war to end." More missiles struck Kyiv late Tuesday, targeting energy systems. Zelenskyy said again that the country received no early warning from partners. “It is important that the world does not stay silent about this,” he posted on X. “And it is important that the United States really see what is happening and who is responsible for this war continuing.” Remarks follow biting criticism from Trump Zelenskyy’s remarks come days after Trump unleashed biting criticism of him, including comments that it was time for a new president in Ukraine and that Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war. The criticism marks perhaps the lowest point in their relationship since their disastrous Oval Office meeting in February 2025. Kyiv continues to rely heavily on Washington for military assistance, including U.S.-made Patriot missile-defense systems and intelligence. The U.S. has the capability to immediately spot Russian ballistic missile launches. American officials have in the past notified Ukraine about launches to allow it to issue missile warnings to the public and to use air defenses against incoming missiles. Asked whether Ukraine received an explanation for the lack of intelligence ahead of the overnight missile strikes, a senior Ukrainian official said it was described as a “failure,” suggesting it was the result of circumstances such as weather conditions rather than a deliberate decision. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to give an official statement on the matter. Ukraine struggles to fend off aerial attacks Russia's war in Ukraine has not seen major shifts on the ground since last year, but Ukraine is struggling to fend off Moscow's intensified aerial attacks that include speedy ballistic missiles and high-flying jet-powered drones . Downing the missiles has been a challenge because of a shortage of Patriot missiles caused by the U.S.-led war in Iran. Russia’s Iskander short-range ballistic missiles take just a few minutes to reach targets in Ukraine. Zelenskyy said Russia had attacked Ukraine with more than 100 weapons since Monday evening. A residential building in the northeastern city of Kharkiv was destroyed, killing four people despite an all-night rescue operation, he said. Russia has increasingly used attacks on civilian infrastructure such as energy facilities to deny Ukrainians power, heat and running water during the 4½-year war, hoping to wear down public support for Ukraine’s response to Moscow’s full-scale invasion. Zelenskyy says Ukraine is respecting energy ceasefire Trump has blamed Ukraine's earlier strikes on Russian oil refineries for record U.S. diesel prices — rather than the war in Iran . He struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday to import diesel from Russia in an attempt to bring fuel prices down ahead of U.S. midterm elections. Meanwhile, Trump claimed Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed on an “energy ceasefire” in which both parties would refrain from striking each other's energy infrastructure. Russia has not confirmed the existence of such a deal. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said only that “contacts on this matter continue.” Zelenskyy on Tuesday said Ukraine had not struck Russian oil refineries or other energy sites in the two days since Trump announced the purported deal. He criticized Moscow for what he said were Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy facilities and infrastructure in the time since Trump's announcement. “The facts show that the Russians do not consider themselves bound by what the President of the United States said,” Zelenskyy said following the attack late Tuesday. The claim that Ukraine has halted its strikes on energy sites could not be independently verified, but neither Russian officials nor media have reported Ukrainian attacks on oil refineries since the energy truce was announced. Strikes on Kharkiv kill 4 and wound 41 Russian strikes across Ukraine caused injuries and deaths overnight Monday and into Tuesday. In addition to the four deaths in the apartment building in Kharkiv, 41 people were wounded in the city in one evening alone, Zelenskyy said. A woman was wounded in a Russian strike on a private home in Kyiv’s Darnytskyi district, the Kyiv city military administration said. A Russian drone hit a residential building in the village of Murovane, near the western city of Lviv, during a morning attack Tuesday, Lviv Mayor Andrii Sadovyi said. One person was killed in the Fastiv district of the Kyiv region, and at least two others were hurt in a Russian attack on the area, said Tymur Tkachenko, head of the regional military administration. A Russian drone struck an educational institution in the center of Rivne in northwest Ukraine, wounding 14 people, according to Oleksandr Koval, head of the Rivne regional military administration. The Russian Defense Ministry said in a statement Tuesday that its forces launched strikes "against Ukrainian military-industrial facilities, logistics centers, railway and port infrastructure, as well as vessels involved in delivering military cargo to Ukraine.” The ministry also said a bulk carrier headed to the port of Mykolaiv with military cargo on board was hit in the estuary of the Bug River along the Black Sea. The Russian Defense Ministry on Tuesday said its air defenses overnight shot down 604 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions and the Sea of Azov. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 417 drones targeted the Moscow region. Most were downed far away, while 65 were intercepted as they approached the Russian capital. A school, two private houses and a car were damaged in the attack in the Kaluga region southwest of Moscow, Gov. Vladislav Shapsha said. ___ Spike reported from Budapest, Hungary. ___ Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/zelenskyy-says-ukraine-received-no-112128424.html

item.title: Trump faces a tough choice after Houthi attacks kill an American in Saudi Arabia
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
London — Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels have dramatically upped the stakes in the complex Middle East war, killing at least 20 people — including an American — and wounding hundreds more with strikes on Saudi Arabia's airports over the last week. The question is whether President Trump will order U.S. military action in support of Saudi Arabia, which has been at war with the rebels in Yemen for more than a decade. Mr. Trump campaigned on ending wars, and he is likely aware, less than a month before the U.S. midterm elections, that opening a new U.S. front in the wider conflict sparked by the Feb. 28 joint U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran could be politically perilous. If he did, he could argue that it is both to protect the Saudis, as a key U.S. ally, and to stop the Iranian proxy group from threatening global shipping in the vital trade routes of the Red Sea. Mr. Trump rejected a request last month by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to join in the kingdom's strikes on the Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News . He came close to ordering airstrikes against the group a week later , but again declined. Asked Sunday if the U.S. would join Saudi strikes, however, the president replied: "We may. We're gonna look at it … We'll make a decision. We move very quickly." So, what has changed, and will it be enough to force Mr. Trump's hand? An American death Little information has come out about the U.S. citizen killed in the Saturday attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, but the killing of an American may increase pressure on Mr. Trump to retaliate. According to Nadwa al-Dawsari, associate fellow at the Middle East Institute, it may not be enough in itself, however, to spur the president to further entrench the U.S. in the wider regional conflict. "I don't think that the killing of an American will trigger a military response," she told CBS News on Monday. "The Houthis have killed American civilians before, including detainees who died after being tortured by the Houthis in Sanaa , and that did not provoke a response from the U.S., militarily or otherwise. Trump's decision will likely depend on his broader assessment of the risks of further escalation." Oil prices Oil prices may be one of the biggest factors in the president's calculus. He has vowed repeatedly to bring down prices at the pump , which have soared as a result of the war with Iran impeding exports from major Persian Gulf energy producers. The Trump administration insists Iran has no control over the Strait of Hormuz, and more oil has been getting out of the Middle East from the Persian Gulf in recent weeks. But the Houthis hold significant territory along Yemen's Red Sea coast, which has enabled them to threaten vessels there and in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the southern gateway to the Red Sea and another key chokepoint for global energy supplies. If the Houthis are able to control Yemen's coastline, or enough of it to maintain their threat to shipping via the Bab el-Mandeb, it would put more pressure on energy flows, increasing the leverage Iran and its proxy groups have over global fuel prices. Thomas Juneau, associate fellow at the Chatham House think tank's Middle East and North Africa Program, told CBS News that this creates "a difficult dilemma for President Trump." "Direct U.S. involvement would likely lead to greater tension in the Red Sea, and therefore create more upward pressure on oil prices," he said. "Should the U.S. refuse to become directly engaged, however, it will cause growing resentment and anger in Saudi Arabia, where feelings of abandonment caused by a widespread perception that the U.S. is failing to support its partner at a time of need are already acute." Helping an ally Despite long-running U.S. accusations that some members of the Saudi leadership supported the al Qaeda Sept. 11 hijackers , and the fallout from the brutal murder of journalist Jamal Khashoggi in 2018, Saudi Arabia has managed to maneuver itself into a position of relative international respectability over the last few years, pursuing a raft of economic reforms to attract foreign investment and building on its status as the world's top oil exporter. The foreign money and visitors could dry up, however, if the Saudis prove incapable of defending themselves from Houthi attacks. Saudi authorities regularly report intercepting Houthi weapons . But the death toll over the last week has exposed gaping holes in Saudi defenses. The Reuters news agency reported Tuesday that the Saudi system to warn civilians of a military attack went silent days before the latest series of deadly Houthi strikes. The Trump administration has fostered close business and defense ties with the Saudis , and failing to come to the aid of an ally in need — especially one that hosts five U.S. military bases — could make Washington appear to be an unreliable ally. What do the Saudis want, and would it be effective? Of all the military options at Mr. Trump's disposal, airstrikes on Houthi targets "would make the greatest difference," al-Dawsari told CBS News. The U.S. has, so far, only acknowledged offering intelligence and targeting support to Saudi Arabia. "The United States can also strengthen air and missile defense cooperation and help identify Houthi launch sites, weapons facilities, and command-and-control infrastructure," al-Dawsari said. While the aim of U.S. strikes would likely be "to degrade the Houthis' ability to launch missiles and drones against Saudi Arabia and threaten shipping in the Red Sea," al-Dawsari said "airstrikes alone will not eliminate the Houthi threat." "The real question is whether American military action would be part of a broader effort to weaken the Houthis, or simply another round of limited strikes that they can absorb and recover from," she said. "The risk is that the United States becomes drawn into a prolonged military campaign against the Houthis while already fighting Iran. But there is also a risk in allowing the Houthis to continue operating as an Iranian military asset and a threat in their own right at Bab el-Mandeb and in the Red Sea," she added. "The United States has a significant interest in keeping the Bab el-Mandeb open, and in protecting the Saudi economy — in particular, the kingdom's ability to export energy products," said CBS News national security analyst Aaron MacLean. "A world in which the Houthis are regularly scoring spectacular hits in Saudi Arabia … is not a world in which America's interests are secure." MacLean cautioned, however, that in addition to the risk of making energy markets even more nervous and driving prices up further, "President Trump has to consider that American military action targeting the Houthis will almost certainly be indecisive." While U.S. strikes could help push the Houthis back and reduce their attack capabilities for a time, "the most Washington can reasonably hope for from a major military operation — adding American airpower to existing capabilities on the ground — is a 'mowing of the lawn,'" said MacLean, and "participating in a protracted conflict with no clear theory of how to end it is a tough sell when you are a president who campaigned on ending so-called 'endless wars.'" The U.S. has targeted the Houthis before , with strikes between March and May 2025 to prevent the group from attacking commercial ships in the Red Sea . The group claimed those attacks were in support of Palestinians, amid Israel's blockade of the Gaza Strip. The U.S. strikes did "cause significant pain to the Houthis … much more than what Saudi Arabia has been able to do," said Juneau, at Chatham House in London. But even those American strikes "were not sufficient to fully deter the Houthis from continuing their attacks in the Red Sea, let alone to defeat them," he said. "The bar for President Trump to authorize strikes now is seemingly pretty high," according to Mona Yacoubian, director of the Middle East Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. "The U.S. is only likely to intercede now in the event of a Houthi attack that results in several U.S. casualties." Asked about the Houthis, President Trump said Monday that the rebels were "misbehaving very badly." He repeated that in a Truth Social post Tuesday, adding that he thought the group "learned their lesson a year ago when we bombed the HELL out of them." "Now they've emerged again, probably at the behest of Iran," Mr. Trump said in the post, adding that the rebels were "in a very nasty way, hitting Saudi Arabia, and purposefully trying to drive up Oil Prices, probably prior to the U.S. Elections — NOT NICE. Somebody should explain to them that I'm not running in the Elections, I've already won, IN A MASSIVE LANDSLIDE, but I'll be there after the Elections, and I will never forget!" In an interview with the French news agency AFP, meanwhile, Houthi political bureau member Mohammed al-Bukhaiti warned Tuesday that if the U.S. chooses to get "involved in the aggression against Yemen, we will not deliberate over the decision to respond, rather, there will be a swift and painful response targeting the U.S. and all its interests in the region." Given the Pentagon's recent acknowledgment of U.S. munitions shortages caused by the war with Iran, Mr. Trump will have to consider carefully the American military's ability to defend against and respond to potential Houthi retaliatory attacks if he does wade into Yemen's civil war.
