item.title: White House press secretary's debut draws criticism but Trump says she was 'very good'
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Katie Zacharia responded after criticism of her first White House press briefing on Tuesday, telling Newsweek via email that “I am grateful to serve President Trump as Press Secretary, and I will diligently and effectively amplify his successful agenda.” During her debut at the podium, Zacharia announced that the White House had asked U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign. Yet much of the reaction to Zacharia’s debut centered on its brevity. She spent just 14 minutes at the podium and took questions from only three outlets before ending the briefing as President Donald Trump prepared to depart the White House for a campaign trip to Alaska. Zacharia, a conservative commentator who most recently worked for Trump’s social media company, was named press secretary on Friday, succeeding Karoline Leavitt , who left the administration in August to spend more time with her family. Her first appearance offered an early glimpse of how Zacharia intends to approach the job. She told reporters that her goal was to “amplify, multiply and expand upon President Trump’s incredible agenda for the American people” while describing Trump as “his own best spokesperson.” Speaking to reporters before his trip to Alaska, Trump responded to a question about Zacharia’s briefing, saying only, “I thought she was very good.” But the brevity of the appearance, along with Zacharia’s delivery and handling of questions, quickly generated criticism from former White House communications officials, journalists and commentators. White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia speaks with reporters in the James Brady Press Briefing Room in the White House on October 13, 2026, in Washington. Katie Zacharia’s 14-Minute White House Briefing Zacharia began the briefing with prepared remarks highlighting Trump’s campaign rallies ahead of the November 3 midterm elections and touting the administration’s record on issues including energy, tariffs and immigration. She took her first question from Breitbart News and said she would continue the “new media” rotation introduced under Leavitt that opened briefing-room access to additional media organizations. Zacharia also made the biggest news of the briefing when she confirmed that Trump had asked Guilfoyle to resign following allegations of improper conduct. “She has been a wonderful asset to the team and we wish her well,” Zacharia said. But after taking questions from only three outlets , including one question about how she plans to balance her family life with the new job, Zacharia brought the briefing to a close as Trump prepared to leave the White House. “In fact, I am going to end it because President Trump is heading out to Marine One for our historic trip to Alaska, and we can ask him all of the questions out there,” she said. Current, Former White House Officials React to Zacharia’s Debut Steven Cheung, the White House director of communications, gave Zacharia high praise after her first appearance in front of the press. He told Newsweek via email: “Katie is a fabulous and wonderful addition to the team. She is uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people about all the great things President Trump and his Administration have been doing, and she will do an incredible job as Press Secretary.” However, some criticism also came from within Trump’s orbit, according to CNN. CNN White House reporter Alayna Treene reported that several White House officials and presidential advisers described Zacharia’s appearance as “awkward” or “stilted,” particularly as she read her opening statement. Trump has shown a willingness to make quick changes to his White House communications operation. The most notable example came in 2017, when Anthony Scaramucci lasted just 10 days as White House communications director . The White House said at the time that Trump believed comments Scaramucci had made about colleagues were inappropriate for someone in his position. Treene noted that Trump publicly praised Zacharia after the briefing and that some people she spoke with believed the president would give his new press secretary the benefit of the doubt. Former Biden White House Communications Director Kate Bedingfield described Zacharia’s performance as a “rocky start” during a CNN appearance on Tuesday. Bedingfield said a press secretary needs to project confidence and demonstrate enough command of administration policy to field questions across a wide range of subjects. “She wasn’t able to do that,” Bedingfield said, while acknowledging that it was Zacharia’s first day. “To send somebody out to the podium who seems incredibly unprepared, unable to answer five, six, seven, eight questions. I mean, typically these briefings can last as long as 45 minutes, an hour.” Bedingfield called the performance “very unimpressive right out of the gate” but also questioned whether Zacharia had been given sufficient time to prepare after being named to the position only four days earlier. “It is unusual for a press secretary to come into the job and go straight out to the podium like that,” Bedingfield said, calling the position “one of the hardest in the entire administration.” WH Press Secretary Katie Zacharia delivers her opening remarks at first press briefing: "I have wanted to work for him for a very long time. I am looking forward to working with each of you as well, especially as we are in the middle of the midterm blitz." pic.twitter.com/aTNHbqc6lM — CSPAN (@cspan) October 13, 2026 Former Biden White House Press Secretary Jen Psaki offered a more blunt assessment. “Well that briefing was basically an SNL skit…except it wasnt…will have a lot more to say at 9pm,” Psaki, now an MS NOW host, wrote on X. The reactions placed immediate scrutiny on Zacharia as she began a job that requires serving as a public face for the administration and managing the White House operation responsible for responding to reporters. Bedingfield argued that the latter responsibility could prove just as consequential as Zacharia’s televised appearances. “The press secretary’s job is only in part what you see on camera,” she said, pointing to running the press shop and overseeing responses to journalists as other major elements of the position. Former Trump White House Deputy Press Secretary Sarah Matthews, who resigned after the January 6, 2021, riot at the U.S. Capitol, also contrasted Zacharia’s debut with predecessors Leavitt and Kayleigh McEnany. “Love them or hate them: Kayleigh McEnany and Karoline Leavitt came out swinging in their first press briefings,” Matthews wrote on X. “They were sharp, confident, prepared, and proved they had the chops for the job right out of the gate.” She described Zacharia’s performance, by comparison, as “a rather underwhelming debut,” pointing to the three questions she took and her “heavy reliance on her notes.” “Not exactly in command of the briefing room,” Matthews added. Former White House press secretary Ari Fleischer, who worked under President George W. Bush, offered a more positive assessment, telling Fox News Tuesday that Zacharia benefited from having substantive announcements to make despite the brevity of her debut. He pointed to her disclosure that Trump had added Kentucky to his upcoming travel schedule and her announcement that the administration had asked Guilfoyle to resign. “There’s nothing that makes the job of the White House press secretary easier than delivering hard news, things that nobody knows about, that your job is to reveal it for the first time on behalf of the president,” Fleischer said. He added that the announcements “gave her substance” and “gave her something serious to talk about, not just talking points.” Fleischer added: “Talking points are indeed an important part of that job, but making news is even more important.” Experts Critique Katie Zacharia’s Performance Democratic strategist Melissa DeRosa also praised Zacharia’s debut during an appearance on Fox News, arguing that the new press secretary avoided becoming the story. “I thought that she presented well,” DeRosa said, adding that Zacharia did not come across as combative as some previous Trump press secretaries. DeRosa said she initially worried that Zacharia’s first appearance could become a “process story,” with observers dissecting her delivery rather than focusing on the administration’s message. Instead, she argued, Zacharia delivered significant news and quickly left the podium. “She came out loaded with news and then she dropped the mic and walked away,” DeRosa said. “I think from a strategic perspective, that was a really smart move.” Beverly Hallberg, president of District Media Group and a senior fellow at the Independent Women’s Forum, also criticized Zacharia’s first appearance while acknowledging the difficulty of making a debut at the White House podium. “There’s grace” for it being Zacharia’s first day, Hallberg wrote on X, but she argued that White House press secretary “isn’t the kind of position where you should be learning on the job.” “You should already be prepared to step into the role, with understandable room to work through the kinks,” Hallberg said. “It’s completely normal for a press secretary to be nervous during her first appearance, but I’m hoping she’ll find her groove because that wasn’t a strong start.” Hallberg, who works as a media coach, focused much of her criticism on Zacharia’s presentation. She said the new press secretary relied too heavily on her notes, spoke too slowly and appeared visibly nervous. She also criticizing Zacharia’s eye contact and tendency to stumble over words. The debut nevertheless underscored one aspect of Zacharia’s philosophy toward the position: She does not intend to compete with Trump for the role of chief messenger. Zacharia explicitly described the president as “his own best spokesperson,” and her decision to end the briefing so reporters could question Trump directly reinforced that approach on her first day behind the lectern. item.title: Trump downplays Russian diesel plan in the face of GOP criticism
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Trump has begun to downplay his new deal with Russia after a plan to allow imports of Russian diesel into the US came under withering criticism, even from members of his own party. "It's a deal for the world ... It's not a deal with me," Trump told reporters on Tuesday morning, repeating that it was "not a USA deal." "They're releasing it to the entire world," Trump added, after making similar comments on Monday that the deal would help US farmers, but said, "It's not really a deal with me, it's a deal for the rest of the world." President Trump speaks to members of the media as he departs the White House on Oct. 13 to travel to Alaska for a rally. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images) Chip Somodevilla via Getty Images The contention is a marked shift since Trump announced the plans last week. "I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia," he wrote on Truth Social , adding that it will be a "great announcement...for Americans and, indeed, the World." The deal will include a quick release of 300,000 tons (about 2.2 million barrels) of diesel. That would then be followed by another 500,000 in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter" for a total of about 13.5 million barrels. His administration quickly authorized US purchases of Russian diesel through next April. Calls on the president to 'immediately reverse course' Blowback to the plan has been notable — even within Trump's own party. A bipartisan group of senators called on the president to "immediately reverse course," in a letter signed by Republican Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina, and John Curtis of Utah, along with three Democrats. The plan has also received a lukewarm reception on the midterm campaign trail, with figures like Republican Mike Rogers, who is locked in a tight Senate contest in Michigan, distancing himself from it . Some energy experts suggest the deal might run afoul of US law, while others suggest it simply won't work since Russia seems to lack enough excess diesel refining capacity to markedly increase exports and move US or global diesel prices. Read more: How oil price shocks ripple through your wallet, from gas to groceries In this pool photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik, Russia's President Vladimir Putin is seen in Moscow on Oct. 11. (Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Pool/AFP via Getty Images) VYACHESLAV PROKOFYEV via Getty Images Indeed, the current average price of diesel, according to the American Automobile Association, was almost $6.28 per gallon on Tuesday, a tick up from almost $6.27 per gallon on Monday. Wholesale diesel prices are "not blinking over Russia/US 'deal'" Patrick De Haan, the head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, noted on Tuesday . "Truckers and farmers not going to see any relief anytime soon." But Trump continued to defend the deal and dodged a question about another major critique, which is that it could fund Russia's war efforts against Ukraine. "Nobody's told me anything," the president said Tuesday in response to whether Russia could use any of the funds to further attack Ukraine. Trump also claimed without evidence that the deal had brought down prices and reaffirmed that his larger goal was to end the overall conflict. He said of Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, "I think they both want it to end, you know, honestly, they both want it to end, and they don't know how to get to that point." item.title: Bank of America hit with $1.2 billion penalty over money laundering failures
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Regulators fined Bank of America ( BAC ) more than $1.2 billion on Tuesday over widespread failures in the banking giant's safeguards against money laundering and other illicit financial activity. The Treasury Department said the nation's second-largest bank failed to properly monitor trillions of dollars in transactions and to report more than $5 billion in suspicious activity, including transactions potentially tied to Chinese money-laundering networks, narcotics trafficking, and fraud. The enforcement actions include a $1.2 billion penalty from the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), the third-largest fine in the Treasury Department's history after it fined crypto exchange Binance $3.4 billion in 2023 and TD Bank for $1.3 billion in 2024. The fine also includes a $750 million penalty from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), the largest ever imposed by that regulator. The OCC penalty will be credited against FinCEN's assessment rather than added to it. Separately, a $11.6 million sanctions settlement brings the total penalties to more than $1.21 billion. "Even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. Bank of America's stock fell more than 2% after markets closed on Tuesday. It reports third quarter earnings Wednesday morning. The bank said it will include a "non-tax-deductible charge of $1.2 billion impacting net income by approximately 17 cents per share" in its third quarter results. "Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right," a Bank of America spokesperson said in an email statement, adding that the Charlotte, North Carolina based lender has invested "billions of dollars in technology" and dedicated "thousands of employees to combat financial crime" to resolve the deficiencies. Regulators said Bank of America's failures extended across its transaction monitoring systems, customer due diligence, and internal oversight. The bank failed to report more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions, including over $1 billion involving national security-related and other priority illicit finance risks. FinCEN said Bank of America admitted to willfully violating the Bank Secrecy Act and had effectively outsourced substantial portions of its suspicious activity detection responsibilities to law enforcement and other financial institutions. The bank also prioritized revenue over compliance resources, according to Treasury, allowing suspicious transactions to go uninvestigated for extended periods. The penalties come nearly two years after Bank of America agreed to a December 2024 cease-and-desist order requiring it to address longstanding weaknesses in its anti-money laundering controls. The OCC said the bank failed to make sufficient progress despite that earlier enforcement action. "Bank of America's poor response to its [Bank Secrecy Act] deficiencies is unacceptable," Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould said, describing continued breakdowns in internal controls. Separately, Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control announced an $11.6 million settlement involving 475 apparent violations of sanctions programs targeting Russia, Iran, and other countries and activities. As part of the latest enforcement actions, Bank of America must conduct a review of previously undetected suspicious transactions with an outside party and undergo independent assessments of its compliance controls. Mike Mayo, a Wells Fargo equity analyst who covers the bank called the action a “black eye” for Bank of America while describing the one-time charge as “digestible.” David Hollerith covers a range of developments throughout the financial sector, from Wall Street to banking and asset management to crypto and fintech. Officials are reviewing the off-base code of conduct for U.S. troops in Japan following the killing of an Okinawan woman, allegedly by a U.S. Marine , Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi said on Tuesday. Crimes including rapes, assaults, hit-and-runs and drunk driving by U.S. military personnel have long triggered protests on the southern Japanese island, which has for years urged other regions of the country to share the burden of hosting U.S. troops. "We plan to hold discussions including whether the existing rules are effectively functioning," Motegi said, adding that "matters such as patrols and curfew management" would be under review in talks with the United States. The high-level bilateral consultations will examine off-duty conduct and the "liberty" policy governing off-base private activities of U.S. military personnel, he said. The existing policy, updated in 2024 following a string of sexual assaults by U.S. military personnel in Okinawa, includes a ban on them drinking in public off-base between 1 a.m. and 5 a.m. or going to bars during those hours. Japanese police arrested a U.S. Marine stationed on Okinawa early this month on suspicion of killing a 39-year-old woman at a hotel in Naha, the capital of Okinawa Orefecture. Word of the arrest drew outrage . The U.S. military enacted a two-day operational pause after the Marine's arrest to reinforce discipline and standards, followed by a monthlong midnight-to-5 a.m. curfew. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said Tuesday that "we began high-level, working-level consultations between Japan and the United States last week on what effective measures should be taken." "The Japanese government will continue to do everything in its power both to address this case and to ensure that it does not happen again," she told a legislative committee session. Motegi spoke by phone over the weekend with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who offered his "sincere condolences" over the alleged crime and pledged U.S. cooperation in the investigation. Crimes committed by U.S. personnel have long been a thorn in relations between the close security allies. A Japanese court sentenced a U.S. Marine accused of choking and attempting to rape a woman in her 20s to seven years in prison last year . In 2017, a former U.S. Marine and civilian military base worker was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa. The United States has approximately 54,000 military personnel stationed in Japan, mostly on Okinawa. item.title: Texas DA says ICE officer intentionally ran over immigrant and may face charges
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
HOUSTON — Videos collected by local investigators make it “pretty obvious” that an ICE officer intentionally ran over Miguel Parra Hernandez during an immigration stop Saturday, which could lead to assault charges, the district attorney said Tuesday. “This was an intentional striking and running over of the person by the vehicle, and in that case, that is an aggravated assault with a deadly weapon in Texas,” Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare told NBC News. Teare said the federal government is not cooperating with the investigation conducted by his office and the Harris County Sheriff’s Office. He also said ICE may have allowed the erasure of critical data in the vehicle involved in striking Parra, who was on foot. Teare said that in his seven years as a Harris County vehicular crimes division chief, he has reviewed video from a number of other auto-pedestrian collision cases. He said the video his investigators have gathered in Parra’s case “goes above” the video that was posted online and obtained by NBC affiliate KPRC of Houston. “My viewing of it, and many other investigators that have viewed it, as well, it’s pretty obvious that this was an intentional striking and running over of the person by the vehicle, and in that case, that is an aggravated assault with a deadly weapon in Texas,” he said. Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare. (Raquel Natalicchio / Houston Chronicle via Getty) Parra, 48, was left with multiple breaks and fractures in his body, according to his attorney and an advocate who has been speaking on his behalf. He had surgery on one leg and faces multiple additional operations, said Cesar Espinosa, co-founder and executive director of FIEL, an immigrant civil rights group. Video obtained by KPRC shows a white truck headed in the opposite direction of traffic on a busy roadway. It shows a vehicle jumping a yellow median and heading in the direction that Parra is running. It then appears to show the vehicle, which is not marked, swerving left toward Parra’s path, in front of a truck stopped in a shopping center. The parked truck leaves, and a man can be seen on the pavement behind the ICE vehicle, the video shows. An ICE spokesman said over the weekend that officers were pursuing the fleeing men and that “Miguel Parra Hernandez ran in front of an ICE vehicle and was struck.” Teare, a Democrat, announced late Monday that his office had launched an independent investigation. On Tuesday, an ICE spokesperson who was not identified said in a statement that “allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are RECKLESS and FALSE. The men and women of ICE are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct.” ICE said the allegations are “disgusting smears” that are “peddled by the media,” leading to more than a 1,600% increase in assaults and a 3,300% increase in vehicle attacks against its law enforcement officers. It did not offer data behind those numbers. ICE has said that Parra was not the target of the attempted stop but that he was in the country illegally. Parra’s attorney and family have said he has no criminal record and was on his way to work applying stucco. Teare said his office and the sheriff’s office determined that the vehicle that struck Parra was a Jeep Cherokee and that it potentially had evidence, including a data crash recorder. He said his office wanted to know whether the vehicle locked in information at the time of the collision that could be downloaded, such as speed, steering and braking. Teare said the way to preserve data from the car would have been to “put it on a flatbed trailer and you take it to forensically download it.” But he said he believes any data on the recorder related to the incident could have been erased when ICE drove the car away. He and the sheriff’s investigators told ICE the information needed to be downloaded, but ICE refused, Teare said. ICE did not respond to questions about a data crash recorder, the erasing of any potential data or any refusal to download it. “Our office began drafting a search warrant that we were in the process of drafting when the ICE agent in question, the one that had been driving, we believed, at the time of the collision, jumped back into the car and drove it away from the scene,” Teare said. “In my 20-year career, I’ve never heard of anything like that.” Teare also said two people from “an entirely different operation” were in the back seat of the ICE vehicle when it struck Parra. Those two people are also in ICE custody, along with Parra. Teare said his office is working to ensure all three remain in the country as material witnesses. “I’ve taught for years at the Houston Police Department Academy, Harris County Department Academy. I’ve worked with law enforcement for 20 years. There is not a single agency in the United States that would teach that once you put people in custody in your car, you then begin to pursue other people,” he said. Doing so puts “every single person out there in danger again,” he said. According to Teare, the ICE vehicle should have activated its emergency equipment, such as its lights and siren, as it jumped a median and crossed into oncoming traffic. A senior official at the Department of Homeland Security told NBC News on Tuesday that multiple ICE officers on the scene at the time were wearing body cameras. ICE is reviewing video of the scene as part of an internal investigation, the official said. Espinosa said Parra told him that he fled because it was unclear whether there were officials in the vehicles, which he said were unmarked, did not use sirens and had dark, tinted windows. ICE has said it was targeting another man, Jose Mendoza Cervantes, who was in the country illegally and had committed several crimes. Parra was struck less than two weeks after the Trump administration issued guidance setting tighter rules for vehicle stops. The guidance says only agents who have completed specific training should make vehicle stops. The memo also says that vehicles used for traffic stops must have lights and sirens and that all officers on the scenes of vehicle stops must wear and activate their body cameras. The Harris County District Attorney’s Office has been asking witnesses and people who may have photos or video of the incident to contact it. Teare said that there is a secure portal that goes directly to the district attorney’s office and that no one is asked about citizenship or immigration status. “All we are interested in is getting the truth, and any shred of cellphone footage, anyone that saw something and really can point us in the right direction, it would be wonderful,” he said. item.title: 'The baby boomers have arrived': Americans over 75 got richer than other age groups
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
For millions of families in the US, wealth has inched up modestly in the last few years, but for older Americans, it's surged. People 75 and older are now the richest group in the US, according to the Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances. The survey, published every three years, found that the median family net worth in the US, adjusted for inflation, rose 2% to $215,900 between 2022 and 2025. But among the 75 and older cohort, their median net worth rose 37% to $505,000, compared with $367,000 in 2022. Families younger than 35, meanwhile, saw their median net worth dive 23% to $33,000. As Mark Zandi, Moody's chief economist, told Yahoo Finance: "The baby boomers have arrived!" "The oldest of the large boomer generation has aged into the 75 and older age group, and the surging stock market has benefited older Americans more because they have more of their wealth in retirement accounts," he said. Wealth inequality on display This isn't startling news given long-held patterns of wealth inequality in America. "On balance, wealth inequality appears little changed since 2022," according to the Fed research. "These changes in wealth largely reinforced existing patterns of wealth inequality by family characteristics." Groups that typically have less wealth — young people, renters, and those without a high school diploma — saw their wealth slip in the years following the pandemic. Families that already had more wealth, whether thanks to age or higher income, saw some of the largest gains. One reason: Higher-income families tend to save more, which in turn helps their wealth grow even more. "Net worth tends to increase and then plateau (or decline) over the life cycle, reflecting changes in savings behavior that occur with age as individuals save for retirement throughout their working career and then spend those savings in retirement," per the report. Importantly, a variety of other factors, aside from age, come into play, including education, race, and whether you've built up equity in a home. For example, when the head of a family had a college degree, they had 1.9 times the median income of those with some college and almost 3 times the median net worth. Stocks and home values lift Americans' net worth It makes sense that many older baby boomers who bought homes and stocks decades ago have seen their assets take off in value. Between the start of 2022 and the end of 2025, the S&P 500 gained roughly 52.41% on a total return basis (including reinvested dividends). For families owning a home, the median net housing value (home value minus debt) rose from $218,900 in 2022 to $230,000 in 2025, according to the Federal Reserve report. Many of those 75 and older may have bought homes when prices were a whisper of what they are today. A typical three-bedroom home in northwest Washington, D.C., for example, purchased three decades ago for under $300,000 could easily have been valued at roughly $1 million in 2025, according to Zillow. "Higher interest rates also helped as this group has a lot of wealth tied up in CDs and other interest-bearing assets," Zandi added. The Social Security factor Social Security is a key factor in older Americans' wealth gains, said Laurence Kotlikoff, a Boston University economics professor and Social Security expert. "Social Security benefits have risen substantially more rapidly than median wages, and that has been happening for some time. People 75-plus who've been able to get Social Security for probably now 13 years, or at least 10 years, have benefited from that as opposed to those who are in the younger age group and on the job," he said. From December 2015 to December 2025, median weekly wages outpaced inflation, according to Pew Research Center data. But over the five years leading up to December 2025, real wages fell after factoring in inflation. Social Security benefits, on the other hand, have increased by a cumulative total of approximately 35.5% over the past 10 years through annual Cost of Living Adjustments (COLA), according to the Social Security Administration. On the flip side: Rising senior poverty While many boomers are truly living their golden years, more seniors are spending them in poverty . Poverty among Americans age 65 and older rose for the fifth consecutive year and has jumped roughly 45% since 2019 — the highest rate of any age group, a recent AARP Foundation analysis of Census data found. That translates to 10 million seniors living in poverty, up from 5.1 million seven years ago. "No other age group has seen that same pattern, and that should really stop us in our tracks. It's alarming," said AARP Foundation president Claire Casey. The poverty slide starts well before age 65. More than 7 million people in their 50s and early 60s are already living in poverty, Casey said. The barriers to saving: healthcare costs, inflation, long-term care, wages failing to keep pace with expenses, and debt. Kerry Hannon is a Senior Columnist at Yahoo Finance. She is a career and retirement strategist and the author of 14 books, including " Retirement Bites: A Gen X Guide to Securing Your Financial Future, " " In Control at 50+: How to Succeed in the New World of Work ," and "Never Too Old to Get Rich." Follow her on Bluesky . item.title: Apple's newest device is entering a market Amazon conquered years ago
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
After months of rumors, Apple is officially (and finally) making its biggest effort yet to grab a piece of the smart home pie. The iPhone maker announced the $299 HomeView on Tuesday, its first smart hub designed to put Siri front-and-center in people's homes. HomeView comes as a countertop device, or a slab you can mount to the wall, both with touchscreens, cameras and the ability to hear and execute Siri voice commands. This is Apple's first dedicated smart home hub ever, and it supports the numerous reports suggesting the company wants to make inroads in the home space. HomeView is designed to be stationary, and it not only connects all of your compatible devices together — things like smart lights, door locks and sensors (including the new Apple Home Collection ) — but also lets you control them using either the on-screen interface or Siri voice commands. But Apple may have a hard time convincing people to add yet another iPad-like screen to their homes, particularly one that emphasizes Siri. The new Siri, known as Siri AI , had a much delayed rollout and is only now available to users with the latest iPhones and devices running iOS 27 . Previously, Siri wasn't the most convenient voice assistant to use, nor the most helpful . Apple has a long way to go to catch up to the likes of Amazon's Alexa and Google's Assistant (now Gemini), and to make up for years of Siri being just meh. Plus, it's very late to the smart display party. To give credit where credit is due: Apple has certainly made progress with Siri. The new Siri AI is better at answering questions with greater detail than before, and it can include personal information from your calendar, Messages and other apps in its answers. This will likely come into play with the HomeView’s ability to recognize different users by their faces via the built-in camera and present personal information to them. But doing things that Alexa and Google have been able to do for a long time is just table stakes at this point. People barely want to use Siri on their iPhones; Apple not only has to prove Siri AI is good enough for people to want to use, period, but now it also has to show it's good enough to justify a separate, $299 device. With continuously skyrocketing tech prices , this may be a particularly tough sell. The fact that Apple is so late here is also working against the company. Amazon's original Echo Show came out in 2017, and Google's first Nest hub debuted in 2018. This isn't the first time Apple came into a space late of course — it has a habit of doing that and still coming out on top — but launching a device like this in 2026 feels a bit stale. Smart home hubs remain important for those building out connected spaces with dozens of devices, but plenty of smart home gear works over Wi-Fi now, no hub required. Privacy could be a selling point for HomeView, and it's an area where Apple has excelled in the past. Indeed, Apple is already emphasizing the privacy aspects of HomeView: the device runs on the A18 chip and includes Secure Enclaves, which are protected and compartmentalized, and process camera and microphone data. According to Apple, data processed by Secure Enclaves "cannot be accessed by the HomeView software, apps, the user, or Apple." Siri requests on HomeView can make use of on-device processing as well as Private Cloud Compute. Apple’s $299 HomeView is available for pre-order today, and will be widely available on November 13. item.title: Trump-appointed judge extends order blocking White House press ban
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A federal judge on Tuesday extended an order blocking President Donald Trump's administration from banning reporters for three news outlets from the White House, a pivotal operational development for the organizations as the extraordinary case — pitting the president against the media that cover him — makes its way through the legal system. In a victory for media organizations at a time when tension between the White House and journalists is high, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ruled that CNN, MS NOW and Politico are likely to succeed in their constitutional free speech and due process claims. “Still,” he added in his late-night order, “no one should interpret the Court’s decision to suggest that President Trump’s concerns about accuracy and fairness in the media’s reporting are unfounded, or that the government is powerless when its true aim is to protect national security when classified information is unlawfully disclosed.” But Kelly agreed with the plaintiffs that the national security arguments came after the fact and were unsupported by the administration. The judge also wrote that without a preliminary injunction the outlets “are likely to suffer irreparable harm, and that the balance of the equities and the public interest tip in their favor.” An email to the Justice Department, which is arguing the case on behalf of the administration, was not immediately returned. The White House also did not immediately respond to an email requesting comment. Theodore Boutrous Jr., attorney for the three media organizations, hailed the judge's ruling. “When the President issued his ‘ban on the free press,’ he blatantly and explicitly violated due process and the First Amendment,” Boutrous said in a statement. “The harm this ban did to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound. The Court was right to enjoin the White House from enforcing this ‘unconstitutional ban on the free press’ for the foreseeable future.” Judge says no warning given before banishment Kelly, who was nominated to the bench by Trump, previously ordered the White House to restore the reporters’ “hard pass” press credentials while he weighed their claims. With that temporary order expiring Tuesday, the judge issued a preliminary injunction that preserves the status quo indefinitely while the case is pending. Kelly said that, “to put it mildly,” the White House didn’t give the plaintiffs any warning that they were in danger of losing their hard passes before Trump’s Sept. 18 social media post about their bans. The judge also said the impact of the White House ban goes far beyond a single reporter's ability to do their job. “The ban threatens to cut off all Plaintiffs’ access to the White House press area—a space open to many of their competitors—thereby restricting their ability to observe happenings there firsthand, immediately report on those activities, and try to engage with government officials,” the judge wrote. Hard passes give journalists who regularly cover the White House longer term access to its campus without having to get permission ahead of time. The government asked Kelly to suspend his own decision pending an appeal, but the judge said it didn’t justify that request. Kelly said the bans impacted a total of 78 reporters at the three news organizations. Earlier judicial action against White House had been only temporary Trump provided no notice before announcing the bans in a Sept. 18 social media post, which criticized their reporting as “fake news.” Kelly temporarily blocked the bans on Sept. 24 at the request of the news outlets, which jointly filed a lawsuit in Washington, D.C. Attorneys for the outlets have described Trump’s move as “unprecedented and blatantly unconstitutional” under the First and Fifth amendments. They argued that it’s illegal for Trump to punish the journalists because he doesn’t like the content of their reporting. “The ban also inflicts an injury on all news media organizations — which now risk a similar fate if they engage in fact-based, independent reporting the President deems insufficiently favorable,” plaintiffs’ lawyers wrote. Government lawyers argued that access to the White House is a privilege — not a right — and said the president can impose the bans to protect national security and to stem the spread of misinformation. “The White House is the official residence and workplace of the President,” Justice Department attorneys wrote . “Presidents have had a relationship with the press since the beginning. They have long decided which journalists should receive privileged access, which has varied substantially from administration to administration.” ___ Associated Press reporter Rebecca Boone contributed. item.title: Mamdani and city council speaker strike deal to ban NYC horse carriage industry
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
NEW YORK — Mayor Zohran Mamdani and New York City Council Speaker Julie Menin have reached a deal to abolish the city's horse carriage industry — a critical breakthrough in a decadeslong, politically fraught effort to ban the tourist attraction. Since 2010, mayors and local legislative leaders have tried to outlaw horse-drawn carriages from operating in Central Park, citing concerns about the safety of the animals as several have died in accidents and from exhaustion. But despite broad popular support, the efforts have failed, in large part due to political pressure from New York's powerful transport union, which advocates for hundreds of carriage drivers who make a living shuttling tourists on buggies around the park. Now, that stalemate appears closer than ever to being broken. In an announcement shared exclusively with POLITICO on Tuesday, a Menin spokesperson said Mamdani's administration has agreed to back a bill that would make it illegal to operate a horse-drawn carriage in the city, starting in June 2028. With Mamdani onboard, Menin — who first announced her support for the bill in July — said she's scheduling a full Council vote on the measure for Oct. 22. The legislation has already secured formal support from more than half of the Council's 51 members, meaning it's on a glidepath to becoming law now that Mamdani is committed to supporting it. "Horse-drawn carriages have long been part of New York City's history, but in an increasingly busy Central Park, this tradition has become a growing public safety liability," Menin said in a statement. "Next week, the Council will take decisive action by voting on [this bill] to protect New Yorkers, visitors, and the horses themselves." Mamdani spokesperson Sneha Choudhary confirmed the mayor and the speaker have reached a deal on the legislation. She also said Mamdani is committed to working on helping carriage drivers find new work and added: "We have been working closely with the City Council, union partners, carriage drivers, animal welfare advocates, and community leaders to deliver a just transition that protects workers while ending horse-drawn carriages in Central Park once and for all." Mamdani and Menin will, no doubt, be hailed by animal rights activists, who have long fought to ban the horse carriage industry, arguing it puts both animals and humans in danger. On the flipside, the announcement isn't without political risk, especially for Mamdani, who has courted support from the Transport Workers Union, which advocates for horse carriage drivers and has been aggressively opposed to any plan that would disband the industry outright. The TWU has pushed for an alternative bill in the Council that would leave the industry in place with new safety regulations. In response to news of the deal, Transport Workers Union International President John Samuelsen, whose New York members are mostly subway, bus and railway workers, blasted the finalized version of the bill for giving "no meaningful economic relief for workers." "This is disgraceful political opportunism, and Zohran should not simply go along with it, particularly when immigrant families' livelihoods are being destroyed," Samuelsen said. "This entire situation is reprehensible." Mamdani has long said he supports the concept of outlawing the horse carriage industry, but prior to Monday, he had withheld support for the Council bill under consideration, arguing it did not go far enough in ensuring protections for the horse carriage drivers who'd lose their livelihoods. Ultimately, Mamdani — a democratic socialist who has positioned himself as a friend of organized labor — came around to backing the bill because the latest version includes several new labor safeguards, according to the speaker's office. Under the updated bill, which was shared with POLITICO, the city must create a workforce transition program under which carriage drivers would receive career counseling as well as referrals to employment opportunities in both public and private sectors, including with the Metropolitan Transportation Authority, the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey, local sight-seeing bus companies and pedicab operators. Additionally, the bill requires the city to "consider" establishing programs to compensate carriage owners for the value of their businesses, their horses, their equipment and the licenses they hold to operate. The bill, which was first introduced by Council member Christopher Marte, notably doesn't require the creation of such programs or earmark a specific amount of money for that purpose, one of several reasons Samuelsen cited in lampooning the bill. "It only says the city should prepare a worker transition plan by April 2027 and include weak measures like job fairs and job counseling. It says the city should 'consider' financial compensation for carriage owners who spent hundreds of thousands of dollars to buy city-issued medallions and build up their businesses," the union head's statement said. According to Menin's office, the speaker will convene a working group focused on addressing any issues that come up during the industry's phase-out period. The speaker will invite the TWU and the mayor's administration to participate in that process. On the other end of the debate, the finalized version of the bill requires carriage horse owners who want to sell their animals to do so in a "humane manner." "A licensed horse may not be sold or otherwise transferred to a person for purposes of slaughter, resale for slaughter, or holding or transport for slaughter, or for use in a horse drawn cab business," a new paragraph inserted into the bill says. The legislation notes that all licensed carriage horse owners must by March 1, 2027, certify to the city that they won't violate the sales restrictions. "This legislation means so much to those who have spent years fighting with us to protect horses and prevent tragedy," said Steve Nislick, co-founding president of New Yorkers for Clean, Livable and Safe Streets, one of the main groups pushing for a carriage ban. "Thanks to Speaker Menin's fortitude and compassion, New York City is finally poised to close this painful chapter." The latest incarnation of the bill began to gain serious momentum over the summer after Romanch Mahajan, an 18-year-old Indian tourist, died when he jumped off a carriage to try to save his mom, who had been flung off the buggy when the horse unexpectedly careened into a gallop. Though many horses have perished in carriage accidents over the years, Mahajan is believed to have been the first human to die in such an accident in modern times. After his death, the bill was renamed "Romanch's Law." The first serious effort to outlaw the city's carriage industry came in 2010, when then-Council Speaker Melissa Mark-Viverito introduced a bill to replace the horse-drawn carriages with electric vehicles. After that bill died during former Mayor Michael Bloomberg's tenure, Bill de Blasio promised as part of his successful 2013 mayoral campaign to enact a ban — but he never made good on that pledge. Former Mayor Eric Adams then also tried to outlaw the carriages in the final months of his term last year. But he too fell short amid resistance from the TWU and Council members aligned with the union.
